questions.question: Radioactive carbon se plant ke reactions kaise trace hue?
questions.hook: Historical puzzle: World War II ke baad radio-activity ko beneficial research tool kaise banaya gaya?

points.point: MELVIN CALVIN born in Minnesota in April, 1911, received his Ph.D. in Chemistry from the University of Minnesota. He served as Professor of Chemistry at the University of California, Berkeley.

Just after world war II, when the world was under shock after the Hiroshima-Nagasaki bombings, and seeing the ill-effects of radio-activity, Calvin and co-workers put radio-activity to beneficial use.
He along with J.A. Bassham studied reactions in green plants forming sugar and other substances from raw materials like carbon dioxide, water and minerals by labelling the carbon dioxide with C¹⁴.
Calvin proposed that plants change light energy to chemical energy by transferring an electron in an organised array of pigment molecules and other substances.
The mapping of the pathway of carbon assimilation in photosynthesis earned him Nobel Prize in 1961.
The principles of photosynthesis as established by Calvin are, at present, being used in studies on renewable resource for energy and materials and basic studies in solar energy research.
Black-and-white photographic portrait of Melvin Calvin, shown from the upper torso upward. The photograph has no scientific labels, arrows or process connections.

1961 Nobel Prize ko carbon-assimilation mapping se jodo; renewable resources aur solar-energy research tak relevance dikhao.

questions.question: Plants food banate hain toh hum un par kaise depend karte hain?
questions.hook: Question: tumhari plate ka food peeche trace karein toh uski shuruaat kahan milegi?

points.point: All animals including human beings depend on plants for their food. Have you ever wondered from where plants get their food? Green plants, in fact, have to make or rather synthesise the food they need
You have already learnt that the autotrophic nutrition is found only in plants and all other organisms that depend on the green plants for food are heterotrophs.
Green plants carry out ‘photosynthesis’, a physico-chemical process by which they use light energy to drive the synthesis of organic compounds.

Ultimately, all living forms on earth depend on sunlight for energy. The use of energy from sunlight by plants doing photosynthesis is the basis of life on earth. Photosynthesis is important due to tw
Have you ever thought what would happen if there were no oxygen to breath [breathe]?
This chapter focusses on the structure of the photosynthetic machinery and the various reactions that transform light energy into chemical energy.

naksha.title: Humare food ki shuruaat kahan hoti hai?
naksha.question: Plants food banate hain toh hum un par kaise depend karte hain?
naksha.prerequisite: Food provides matter and energy; consumers obtain food by feeding.
naksha.opens_with: Question: tumhari plate ka food peeche trace karein toh uski shuruaat kahan milegi?
story: Worked example: green plant → grazing animal → human food dependence trace karo.
Autotroph organic food synthesise karta hai; mineral absorption ko food synthesis mat samjho.
Photosynthesis ki physico-chemical definition kholo: light energy organic-compound synthesis drive karti hai; carbon aur energy inputs alag hain.
Food production aur atmospheric oxygen release, dono importance batao; sunlight-dependence ko chapter ke ecological context mein rakho, universal exceptionless claim nahi.
Oxygen na ho toh kya hoga pose karke answer do: aerobic cellular energy supply severely affected hogi.
Apne words mein roadmap do: machinery aur energy-converting reactions padhenge; abhi organelle tour nahi.

real_world: Plant-derived food human diets aur livestock feeding ko support karta hai.

outside_book.why: Printed plant-only autotrophy aur all-life sunlight statements ko absolute misconception banne se rokna.

naksha.title: Leaf ke starch test se requirements kaise prove hoti hain?
naksha.question: Chlorophyll, light aur CO₂ zaroori hain, yeh evidence se kaise bolenge?
naksha.prerequisite: Controlled comparisons; iodine starch test ka short demonstration.
naksha.opens_with: Experiment: ek variegated leaf aur ek black-paper-covered leaf ko light mein rakho—starch kahan milega?
story: Green versus non-green regions chlorophyll ko, covered versus uncovered regions light ko test karte hain.
Worked example: matched leaf maps par starch-positive regions mark karo; purana starch hataane ke liye destarching ka reason batao.
KOH-soaked cotton wala test-tube setup dekho: enclosed leaf portion se CO₂ remove hota hai, outside portion ko air milti hai.
Conclusion wala in-text question pose aur answer karo: comparable illuminated portions mein CO₂-deprived region negative aur exposed region positive hona CO₂ requirement support karta hai.
Starch indirect evidence hai; requirements ki recalled list water ko unnecessary nahi banati.

analogy.picture: Ek hi setting mein ek switch badalna.
analogy.why_it_fits: Inference tab strong hota hai jab relevant difference sirf tested condition ho.

examples: Variegated leaf aur partly black-paper-covered leaf ke starch maps compare karo; phir ek leaf ke KOH-enclosed aur air-exposed portions se CO₂ requirement infer karo.

outside_book.why: Old starch confounding aur chemical-safety risk se bachna; teacher-supervised demonstration banana.

questions.question: Priestley aur Ingenhousz ke experiments ne alag-alag kya dikhaya?
questions.hook: Scene: band bell jar mein candle bujh gayi—mint plant add karne se result kyun badal sakta hai?

points.point: It is interesting to learn about those simple experiments that led to a gradual development in our understanding of photosynthesis.
Joseph Priestley (1733-1804) in 1770 performed a series of experiments that revealed the essential role of air in the growth of green plants. Priestley, you may recall, discovered oxygen in 1774.

Priestley observed that a candle burning in a closed space – a bell jar, soon gets extinguished (Figure 11.1 a, b, c, d). Similarly, a mouse would soon suffocate in a closed space. He concluded that a

Figure 11.1 shows four bell-jar panels. Upper row: (a) a mouse and a burning candle are enclosed without a plant; a rightward arrow leads to (b), showing an unlit candle and a collapsed mouse. Lower r

Can you imagine how Priestley would have conducted the experiment using a candle and a plant? Remember, he would need to rekindle the candle to test whether it burns after a few days. How many differe
Using a similar setup as the one used by Priestley, but by placing it once in the dark and once in the sunlight, Jan Ingenhousz (1730-1799) showed that sunlight is essential to the plant process that

Ingenhousz in an elegant experiment with an aquatic plant showed that in bright sunlight, small bubbles were formed around the green parts while in the dark they did not. Later he identified these bub

naksha.title: Plants air ko kab restore karte hain?
naksha.question: Priestley aur Ingenhousz ke experiments ne alag-alag kya dikhaya?
naksha.prerequisite: Burning aur animal respiration oxygen consume karte hain; closed jars freely air exchange nahi karte.
naksha.opens_with: Scene: band bell jar mein candle bujh gayi—mint plant add karne se result kyun badal sakta hai?
story: History ko questions ki sequence banao: Priestley 1770 bell jars; oxygen discovery 1774 alag milestone.
Worked example: Figure 11.1 ke a→b aur c→d horizontal pairs compare karo, a→b→c→d sequence nahi.
Mint experiment se restoration-of-air hypothesis nikalo; modern oxygen interpretation ko historical wording se distinguish karo.
Jar khole bina rekindling question answer karo: teacher-controlled lens se sunlight focus karna ya sealed electrical ignition possible designs hain; live-animal replication nahi.
Ingenhousz ke dark/sunlight comparison se sunlight requirement aur unnamed aquatic plant ke green parts par oxygen bubbles se tissue restriction samjhao.
Plants ko passive air filters mat bolo; respiration aur illuminated photosynthesis ke net effects distinguish karo.

analogy.picture: Shared oxygen account mein withdrawals aur replenishment.
analogy.why_it_fits: Burning aur respiration oxygen ghataate hain, illuminated photosynthesis replenish kar sakti hai.

examples: Priestley ke mint plant, mouse aur candle wale bell jars ke do separate before–after pairs se air-restoration hypothesis nikalo; Ingenhousz ka light–dark control usmein kya add karta hai, batao.
real_world: Sunlit aquatic vegetation ke paas oxygen bubbles observe kiye ja sakte hain.

outside_book.what: Sealed electrical ignition ya lens-focussed sunlight as possible rekindling designs; simulations instead of animal experiments.
outside_book.why: In-text design question ka answer aur safe, ethical classroom treatment.

saman.shows: Figure 11.1 ke four panels, sirf do horizontal arrows aur mint-plant comparison.
saman.why: Conditions, outcomes aur undisturbed testing ka logic clear hota hai.

saman.shows: Same aquatic-plant setup light aur dark mein, green tissues ke bubbles highlighted.
saman.why: Ingenhousz ke additional controls aur conclusion alag dikhte hain.

questions.question: Photosynthesis equation mein 12 water kyun hain, aur O₂ ka source kya hai?
questions.hook: Number puzzle: equation ke left par 12H₂O, right par 6H₂O—net water kitna gaya?

points.point:
CO₂ + H₂O —Light→ [CH₂O] + O₂
where [CH₂O] represented a carbohydrate (e.g., glucose, a six-carbon sugar).
A milestone contribution to the understanding of photosynthesis was that made by a microbiologist, Cornelius van Niel (1897-1985), who, based on his studies of purple and green bacteria, demonstrated
2H₂A + CO₂ —Light→ 2A + CH₂O + H₂O
In green plants H₂O is the hydrogen donor and is oxidised to O₂. Some organisms do not release O₂ during photosynthesis. When H₂S, instead is the hydrogen donor for purple and green sulphur bacteria,

and not O₂. Hence, he inferred that the O₂ evolved by the green plant comes from H₂O, not from carbon dioxide. This was later proved by using radioisotopic techniques. The correct equation, that would
6CO₂ + 12H₂O —Light→ C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6H₂O + 6O₂
where C₆H₁₂O₆ represents glucose. The O₂ released is from water; this was proved using radio isotope techniques. Note that this is not a single
reaction but description of a multistep process called photosynthesis.
Can you explain why twelve molecules of water as substrate are used in the equation given above?

Balanced plant equation ke atoms count karo; 12 gross input waters mein se 6 net consumed hain. Six O₂ formation ke electron accounting mein 12 waters oxidised hote hain, aur overall reduction accounting mein 6 waters reappear karte hain.

Several protein complexes are involved in the process. The pigments are organised into two discrete photochemical light harvesting complexes (LHC) within the Photosystem I (PS I) and Photosystem II (P

The LHC are made up of hundreds of pigment molecules bound to proteins. Each photosystem has all the pigments (except one molecule of chlorophyll a) forming a light harvesting system also called anten

The light harvesting complex is drawn as a cluster of green pigment molecules. A red incoming photon strikes a peripheral pigment. A red zigzag route passes through the pigment cluster towards the rea

The single chlorophyll a molecule forms the reaction centre. The reaction centre is different in both the photosystems. In PS I the reaction centre chlorophyll a has an absorption peak at 700 nm, henc

questions.question: Water splitting se electrons, oxygen aur protons kahan milte hain?
questions.hook: In-text sawaal: PS II electron bhejta rahe toh uski supply khatam kyun nahi hoti?

points.point: You would then ask, How does PS II supply electrons continuously? The

electrons that were moved from photosystem II must be replaced. This is achieved by electrons available due to splitting of water. The splitting of water is associated with the PS II; water is split i
2H₂O → 4H⁺ + O₂ + 4e⁻
We need to emphasise here that the water splitting complex is associated with the PS II, which itself is physically located on the inner side of the membrane of the thylakoid.
Then, where are the protons and O₂ formed likely to be released – in the lumen? or on the outer side of the membrane?

film.showing_moment: Lumen-facing PS II complex; two water molecules se counted products aur electron-replacement arrows.

naksha.title: PS II ke lost electrons kaun replace karta hai?

story: Answer do: PS II-associated water splitting replacement electrons deti hai; PS II transport chain se PS I ko replenish karta hai.
Worked example: 2H₂O ko 4H⁺ + O₂ + 4e⁻ mein balance karo; atoms aur charge count karo.
Local thylakoid cross-section mein water-splitting complex lumen-facing side par place karo.
Protons aur O₂ kahan release honge question pose aur answer karo: lumen side; O₂ baad mein diffuse kar sakti hai.
Water source ko ek sentence mein recall karo; historical proof dobara teach nahi.

analogy.picture: Chalti line ke starting slot mein naya token bharna.
analogy.why_it_fits: Continuous outward transfer ke liye donor se replenishment zaroori hai.

examples: Do water molecule models split karke 4H⁺, ek O₂ aur 4e⁻ count karo; electrons PS II ko aur protons lumen side ko route karo.
real_world: Green plants ka evolved atmospheric oxygen water oxidation se originate hota hai.

points.point: Why are we so interested in the proton gradient?

This gradient is important because it is the breakdown of this gradient that leads to the synthesis of ATP. The gradient is broken down due to the movement of protons across the membrane to the stroma

channel of the CF₀ of the ATP synthase. The ATP synthase enzyme consists of two parts: one called the CF₀ is embedded in the thylakoid membrane and forms a transmembrane channel that carries out facil

The break down of the gradient provides enough energy to cause a conformational change in the CF₁ particle of the ATP synthase, which makes the enzyme synthesise several molecules of energy-packed ATP

Chemiosmosis requires a membrane, a proton pump, a proton gradient and ATP synthase. Energy is used to pump protons across a membrane, to create a gradient or a high concentration of protons within th

Along with the NADPH produced by the movement of electrons, the ATP will be used immediately in the biosynthetic reaction taking place in the stroma, responsible for fixing CO₂, and synthesis of sugar

questions.hook: Cycle puzzle: acceptor har turn mein use hota hai toh next CO₂ ke liye acceptor kahan se aata hai?

points.point: Calvin and his co-workers then worked out the whole pathway and showed that the pathway operated in a cyclic manner; the RuBP was regenerated.

Let us now see how the Calvin pathway operates and where the sugar is synthesised. Let us at the outset understand very clearly that the Calvin pathway occurs in all photosynthetic plants; it does not
For ease of understanding, the Calvin cycle can be described under three stages: carboxylation, reduction and regeneration.

1. Carboxylation – Carboxylation is the fixation of CO₂ into a stable organic intermediate. Carboxylation is the most crucial step of the Calvin cycle where CO₂ is utilised for the carboxylation of Ru

Calvin cycle: atmospheric CO₂ + H₂O enters stage 1, Carboxylation, with ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate. The clockwise path proceeds to 3-phosphoglycerate, then stage 2, Reduction, then triose phosphate. AT

2. Reduction – These are a series of reactions that lead to the formation of glucose. The steps involve utilisation of 2 molecules of ATP for phosphorylation and two of NADPH for reduction per CO₂ mol
3. Regeneration – Regeneration of the CO₂ acceptor molecule RuBP is crucial if the cycle is to continue uninterrupted. The regeneration steps require one ATP for phosphorylation to form RuBP.

points.point: Now study the pathway shown in Figure 11.9. This pathway that has been named the Hatch and Slack Pathway, is again a cyclic process. Let us study the pathway by listing the steps.

The primary CO₂ acceptor is a 3-carbon molecule phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP) and is present in the mesophyll cells. The enzyme responsible for this fixation is PEP carboxylase or PEPcase. It is importan

It then forms other 4-carbon compounds like malic acid or aspartic acid in the mesophyll cells itself, which are transported to the bundle sheath cells. In the bundle sheath cells these C₄ acids are b
The 3-carbon molecule is transported back to the mesophyll where it is converted to PEP again, thus, completing the cycle.
The CO₂ released in the bundle sheath cells enters the C₃ or the Calvin pathway, a pathway common to all plants. The bundle sheath cells are

Two connected cells show the Hatch and Slack pathway. The upper mesophyll cell receives atmospheric CO₂, shown as HCO₃⁻ joining phosphoenol-pyruvate at Fixation. A downward arrow leads to C₄ acid, the
rich in an enzyme Ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase (RuBisCO), but lack PEPcase. Thus, the basic pathway that results in the formation of the sugars, the Calvin pathway, is common to the C₃
Did you note that the Calvin pathway occurs in all the mesophyll cells of the C₃ plants? In the C₄ plants it does not take place in the mesophyll cells but does so only in the bundle sheath cells.

story: Opening lines aur boxed normal reaction ko already-taught baseline ke quick checkpoint ki tarah use karo; carboxylation ka fresh lecture nahi.
Most abundant enzyme aur dual active-site binding ke embedded questions answer karo: photosynthetic carbon fixation ki huge demand aur alternative substrate reactions ka concept.

Photorespiratory account: ATP used, CO₂ released; no sugar, ATP or NADPH synthesis. Book ka biological-function statement as textbook account quote karo, universal modern conclusion nahi.

questions.hook: Three-control challenge: lamp ka colour, brightness aur on-time—teeno mein se intensity graph kya badalta hai?

points.point: We need to distinguish between light quality, light intensity and the duration of exposure to light, while discussing light as a factor that affects photosynthesis.

There is a linear relationship between incident light and CO₂ fixation rates at low light intensities. At higher light intensities, gradually the rate does not show further increase as other factors b
What is interesting to note is that light saturation occurs at 10 per cent of the full sunlight. Hence, except for plants in shade or in dense forests, light is rarely a limiting factor in nature.

The description of structure and variation of living organisms over a period of time, ended up as two, apparently irreconcilable perspectives on biology. The two perspectives essentially rested on two

Description of physiological processes, in flowering plants as an example, is what is given in the chapters in this unit. The processes of photosynthesis, respiration and ultimately plant growth and d
MELVIN CALVIN born in Minnesota in April, 1911, received his Ph.D. in Chemistry from the University of Minnesota. He served as Professor of Chemistry at the University of California, Berkeley.

Just after world war II, when the world was under shock after the Hiroshima-Nagasaki bombings, and seeing the ill-effects of radio-activity, Calvin and co-workers put radio-activity to beneficial use.
He along with J.A. Bassham studied reactions in green plants forming sugar and other substances from raw materials like carbon dioxide, water and minerals by labelling the carbon dioxide with C¹⁴.
Calvin proposed that plants change light energy to chemical energy by transferring an electron in an organised array of pigment molecules and other substances.
The mapping of the pathway of carbon assimilation in photosynthesis earned him Nobel Prize in 1961.
The principles of photosynthesis as established by Calvin are, at present, being used in studies on renewable resource for energy and materials and basic studies in solar energy research.
Black-and-white photographic portrait of Melvin Calvin, shown from the upper torso upward. The photograph has no scientific labels, arrows or process connections.

All animals including human beings depend on plants for their food. Have you ever wondered from where plants get their food? Green plants, in fact, have to make or rather synthesise the food they need
You have already learnt that the autotrophic nutrition is found only in plants and all other organisms that depend on the green plants for food are heterotrophs.
Green plants carry out ‘photosynthesis’, a physico-chemical process by which they use light energy to drive the synthesis of organic compounds.

Ultimately, all living forms on earth depend on sunlight for energy. The use of energy from sunlight by plants doing photosynthesis is the basis of life on earth. Photosynthesis is important due to tw
Have you ever thought what would happen if there were no oxygen to breath [breathe]?
This chapter focusses on the structure of the photosynthetic machinery and the various reactions that transform light energy into chemical energy.

questions.hook: 1770 ka bell jar: mint plant ke saath candle ka outcome kyun badla?

points.point: It is interesting to learn about those simple experiments that led to a gradual development in our understanding of photosynthesis.
Joseph Priestley (1733-1804) in 1770 performed a series of experiments that revealed the essential role of air in the growth of green plants. Priestley, you may recall, discovered oxygen in 1774.

Priestley observed that a candle burning in a closed space – a bell jar, soon gets extinguished (Figure 11.1 a, b, c, d). Similarly, a mouse would soon suffocate in a closed space. He concluded that a

Figure 11.1 shows four bell-jar panels. Upper row: (a) a mouse and a burning candle are enclosed without a plant; a rightward arrow leads to (b), showing an unlit candle and a collapsed mouse. Lower r

Can you imagine how Priestley would have conducted the experiment using a candle and a plant? Remember, he would need to rekindle the candle to test whether it burns after a few days. How many differe
Using a similar setup as the one used by Priestley, but by placing it once in the dark and once in the sunlight, Jan Ingenhousz (1730-1799) showed that sunlight is essential to the plant process that

Ingenhousz in an elegant experiment with an aquatic plant showed that in bright sunlight, small bubbles were formed around the green parts while in the dark they did not. Later he identified these bub

It was not until about 1854 that Julius von Sachs provided evidence for production of glucose when plants grow. Glucose is usually stored as starch. His later studies showed that the green substance i

Now consider the interesting experiments done by T.W Engelmann (1843 – 1909). Using a prism he split light into its spectral components and then illuminated a green alga, Cladophora, placed in a suspe

By the middle of the nineteenth century the key features of plant photosynthesis were known, namely, that plants could use light energy to make carbohydrates from CO₂ and water. The empirical equation

CO₂ + H₂O —Light→ [CH₂O] + O₂
where [CH₂O] represented a carbohydrate (e.g., glucose, a six-carbon sugar).
A milestone contribution to the understanding of photosynthesis was that made by a microbiologist, Cornelius van Niel (1897-1985), who, based on his studies of purple and green bacteria, demonstrated
2H₂A + CO₂ —Light→ 2A + CH₂O + H₂O
In green plants H₂O is the hydrogen donor and is oxidised to O₂. Some organisms do not release O₂ during photosynthesis. When H₂S, instead is the hydrogen donor for purple and green sulphur bacteria,

and not O₂. Hence, he inferred that the O₂ evolved by the green plant comes from H₂O, not from carbon dioxide. This was later proved by using radioisotopic techniques. The correct equation, that would
6CO₂ + 12H₂O —Light→ C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6H₂O + 6O₂
where C₆H₁₂O₆ represents glucose. The O₂ released is from water; this was proved using radio isotope techniques. Note that this is not a single
reaction but description of a multistep process called photosynthesis.
Can you explain why twelve molecules of water as substrate are used in the equation given above?

points.point: Calvin and his co-workers then worked out the whole pathway and showed that the pathway operated in a cyclic manner; the RuBP was regenerated.

Let us now see how the Calvin pathway operates and where the sugar is synthesised. Let us at the outset understand very clearly that the Calvin pathway occurs in all photosynthetic plants; it does not
For ease of understanding, the Calvin cycle can be described under three stages: carboxylation, reduction and regeneration.

1. Carboxylation – Carboxylation is the fixation of CO₂ into a stable organic intermediate. Carboxylation is the most crucial step of the Calvin cycle where CO₂ is utilised for the carboxylation of Ru

Calvin cycle: atmospheric CO₂ + H₂O enters stage 1, Carboxylation, with ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate. The clockwise path proceeds to 3-phosphoglycerate, then stage 2, Reduction, then triose phosphate. AT

2. Reduction – These are a series of reactions that lead to the formation of glucose. The steps involve utilisation of 2 molecules of ATP for phosphorylation and two of NADPH for reduction per CO₂ mol
3. Regeneration – Regeneration of the CO₂ acceptor molecule RuBP is crucial if the cycle is to continue uninterrupted. The regeneration steps require one ATP for phosphorylation to form RuBP.

Hence for every CO₂ molecule entering the Calvin cycle, 3 molecules of ATP and 2 of NADPH are required. It is probably to meet this difference in number of ATP and NADPH used in the dark reaction that
To make one molecule of glucose 6 turns of the cycle are required.
Work out how many ATP and NADPH molecules will be required to make one molecule of glucose through the Calvin pathway.
It might help you to understand all of this if we look at what goes in and what comes out of the Calvin cycle.

points.point: Plants that are adapted to dry tropical regions have the C₄ pathway mentioned earlier. Though these plants have the C₄ oxaloacetic acid as the first CO₂ fixation product they use the C₃ pathway or the
as the main biosynthetic pathway. Then, in what way are they different from C₃ plants? This is a question that you may reasonably ask.

C₄ plants are special: They have a special type of leaf anatomy, they tolerate higher temperatures, they show a response to high light intensities, they lack a process called photorespiration and have

Study vertical sections of leaves, one of a C₃ plant and the other of a C₄ plant. Do you notice the differences? Do both have the same types of mesophylls? Do they have similar cells around the vascul

The particularly large cells around the vascular bundles of the C₄ plants are called bundle sheath cells, and the leaves which have such anatomy are said to have ‘Kranz’ anatomy. ‘Kranz’ means ‘wreath

The bundle sheath cells may form several layers around the vascular bundles; they are characterised by having a large number of chloroplasts, thick walls impervious to gaseous exchange and no intercel
You may like to cut a section of the leaves of C₄ plants – maize or sorghum – to observe the Kranz anatomy and the distribution of mesophyll cells.
It would be interesting for you to collect leaves of diverse species of plants around you and cut vertical sections of the leaves. Observe under the microscope – look for the bundle sheath around the
Now study the pathway shown in Figure 11.9. This pathway that has been named the Hatch and Slack Pathway, is again a cyclic process. Let us study the pathway by listing the steps.

The primary CO₂ acceptor is a 3-carbon molecule phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP) and is present in the mesophyll cells. The enzyme responsible for this fixation is PEP carboxylase or PEPcase. It is importan

It then forms other 4-carbon compounds like malic acid or aspartic acid in the mesophyll cells itself, which are transported to the bundle sheath cells. In the bundle sheath cells these C₄ acids are b
The 3-carbon molecule is transported back to the mesophyll where it is converted to PEP again, thus, completing the cycle.
The CO₂ released in the bundle sheath cells enters the C₃ or the Calvin pathway, a pathway common to all plants. The bundle sheath cells are

Two connected cells show the Hatch and Slack pathway. The upper mesophyll cell receives atmospheric CO₂, shown as HCO₃⁻ joining phosphoenol-pyruvate at Fixation. A downward arrow leads to C₄ acid, the
rich in an enzyme Ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase (RuBisCO), but lack PEPcase. Thus, the basic pathway that results in the formation of the sugars, the Calvin pathway, is common to the C₃
Did you note that the Calvin pathway occurs in all the mesophyll cells of the C₃ plants? In the C₄ plants it does not take place in the mesophyll cells but does so only in the bundle sheath cells.

questions.hook: Lamp ka colour, brightness aur timer—graph mein kaunsa badal raha hai?

points.point: We need to distinguish between light quality, light intensity and the duration of exposure to light, while discussing light as a factor that affects photosynthesis.

There is a linear relationship between incident light and CO₂ fixation rates at low light intensities. At higher light intensities, gradually the rate does not show further increase as other factors b
What is interesting to note is that light saturation occurs at 10 per cent of the full sunlight. Hence, except for plants in shade or in dense forests, light is rarely a limiting factor in nature.
